title: Commutative extensions of additive subgroups are Witt pullbacks
statement: Let $k$ be a perfect field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$, meaning every element of $k$ is a $p$-th power. Let $Q\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_a$ be a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sc-gm-ga], and let $0\to\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{i}E\xrightarrow{q}Q\to0$ be an exact sequence of commutative affine finite-type $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Exact means $i$ identifies $\mathbf G_a$ with the scheme-theoretic kernel of $q$ and $q$ is faithfully flat and finitely presented, equivalently the sequence of represented fppf sheaves is short exact for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $k$-algebras. Let $j,\tau,W_{2,k}$ denote the two-coordinate Witt extension of [lem-sfb-length-two-witt-extension-verschiebung]. There exist a group-scheme homomorphism $h:Q\to\mathbf G_a$ and an isomorphism of extensions $E\simeq Q\times_{\mathbf G_a,h,\tau}W_{2,k}$ [def-pc-fibre-product], inducing the identity on the kernel $\mathbf G_a$ and quotient $Q$. In particular the second projection gives $a:E\to W_{2,k}$ with $\tau a=hq$ and $ai=j$. The zero homomorphism $h=0$ is allowed, so this includes split extensions. No smoothness or connectedness of $Q$ or $E$ is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 15.27, printed p.316, including its displayed extension (113). The perfect-field restriction is sufficient for its use in the proof of Proposition 14.48, printed p.296.

proof.text: Translation by the kernel makes $q:E\to Q$ an additive torsor. Indeed, $(e,t)\mapsto(e,e+i(t))$ has inverse $(e,e')\mapsto(e,i^{-1}(e'-e))$ on $E\times_QE$: the difference belongs to the scheme-theoretic kernel, so its factorization through $i$ is unique and is a morphism. Apply [lem-sfb-additive-affine-torsor-section] to the affine base $Q$. Its covering hypotheses are exactly the stipulated faithful flatness and finite presentation of $q$. Choose a section $s$, and replace it by $s-i(s(0))$ to arrange $s(0)=0$ (here $s(0)$ is identified with its unique kernel coordinate). The maps $(t,x)\mapsto i(t)+s(x)$ and $e\mapsto(i^{-1}(e-s(q(e))),q(e))$ are inverse scheme morphisms. Thus $E$ has coordinates $\mathbf G_a\times Q$, preserving the specified kernel and quotient.

source.place: Proposition 15.27, first two sentences; Example 2.72; Proposition 15.10, choice of section.

proof.text:
In these coordinates define $f:Q\times Q\to\mathbf G_a$ by $s(x)+s(y)=i(f(x,y))+s(x+y)$. Commutativity, associativity, and $s(0)=0$ give, respectively,
$$f(x,y)=f(y,x),\quad f(y,z)-f(x+y,z)+f(x,y+z)-f(x,y)=0,\quad f(x,0)=f(0,x)=0.$$
The group law is $(t,x)+(u,y)=(t+u+f(x,y),x+y)$. These are identities of morphisms, hence of regular functions, not just of $k$-points. The affine-spectrum and polynomial universal properties identify regular functions on $Q^m$ with the corresponding coordinate polynomials modulo its defining ideal in each variable: maps to the product are tuples of algebra maps agreeing on $k$, which is exactly the universal property of that polynomial quotient. If $Q=\mathbf G_a$, this gives a normalized symmetric polynomial cocycle $F=f\in k[X,Y]$.

source.place: Proposition 15.10 and Corollary 15.11, pp.308-309; Proposition 15.27, Hochschild-extension reduction.

proof.text: If $Q\ne\mathbf G_a$, apply [lem-sfb-additive-subgroup-polynomial-quotient] to get $k[Q]=k[T]/(P)$ with $P$ monic of degree $n>0$ and $P(0)=0$. The monic quotient basis [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free], successively in each variable over the other coefficient rings, gives a unique representative $F\in k[X,Y]$ of $f$ with both variable degrees $<n$. Symmetry and normalization hold before reduction: swapping variables, or setting one to zero, preserves these degree bounds, and uniqueness of remainders applies. Put $D=F(Y,Z)-F(X+Y,Z)+F(X,Y+Z)-F(X,Y)$. Each variable in $D$ has degree $<n$, since substituting $X+Y$ into a monomial of exponent $<n$ never gives either variable an exponent $\geq n$. Its residue modulo $(P(X),P(Y),P(Z))$ is zero by step 2. Successive uniqueness of monic remainders implies $D=0$ in $k[X,Y,Z]$. Thus in both cases a normalized symmetric polynomial cocycle $F$ on the whole additive line restricts to $f$ on $Q^2$. This argument includes nonreduced $Q$.

source.place: Proposition 15.27, last four sentences, pp.316-317: the bounded-degree lift in U tensor U.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-symmetric-polynomial-cocycle-normal-form] to $F$. Obtain $F=\sum_{i=0}^r a_i c_p(X,Y)^{p^i}+\delta b$, where $\delta b=b(X)+b(Y)-b(X+Y)$ and $b(0)=0$. This is a polynomial identity over $k$; restrict it to $Q^2$. Choose $b_i\in k$ with $b_i^p=a_i$, using perfectness, and set $h(T)=\sum_{i=0}^r b_i T^{p^i}$. The binomial identity in characteristic $p$ shows $h(X+Y)=h(X)+h(Y)$, so its restriction to $Q$ is a group-scheme homomorphism $Q\to\mathbf G_a$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26 and Proposition 15.27, the End(G_a) step, using 14.40; perfect-field specialization.

proof.text:
Use the commutative group law of [lem-sfb-length-two-witt-extension-verschiebung]. Define a polynomial $B(T)$ by the finite sum in $W_{2,k}$
$$\sum_{i=0}^r (b_iT^{p^i},0)=(h(T),B(T));$$
it is obtained by repeated substitution in the displayed polynomial law and $B(0)=0$. Regrouping the sum of these vectors at $X$ and $Y$ in two ways gives
$$B(X)+B(Y)+c_p(h(X),h(Y))=B(X+Y)+\sum_i a_i c_p(X,Y)^{p^i}.$$
Indeed, for each $i$ the paired summands have first coordinate $b_i(X+Y)^{p^i}$ and second coordinate $c_p(b_iX^{p^i},b_iY^{p^i})=b_i^p c_p(X,Y)^{p^i}$: $c_p$ is homogeneous of degree $p$ with coefficients in the prime field. The extra second coordinates add because $(0,v)$ is central and its addition has no cross term. Therefore $F=c_p(h(X),h(Y))+\delta(b+B)$. This supplies the correction term rather than identifying an arbitrary linear combination of Witt classes with a single pullback without justification.

source.place: Proposition 15.27, the implication from Lemma 15.26 via End(G_a); explicit addition of the displayed Witt extension (113).

proof.text:
Let $u=(b+B)|_Q$. The fibre product in the conclusion has points $(x,(h(x),v))$, with group law on its $(v,x)$ coordinates given by $c_p(h(x),h(y))$. The identity from step 5 restricted to $Q^2$ says $f(x,y)=c_p(h(x),h(y))+u(x)+u(y)-u(x+y)$. Thus
$$i(t)+s(x)\longmapsto (x,(h(x),t+u(x)))$$
is a homomorphism to that fibre product: the two second-coordinate expressions agree by this identity. It has the regular inverse $(x,(h(x),v))\mapsto i(v-u(x))+s(x)$. The affine-spectrum and fibre-product universal properties make these scheme morphisms and prove that their composites are identities. Since $h(0)=u(0)=0$, this isomorphism is the identity on the specified kernel and quotient. Its second projection is $a$, so $\tau a=hq$ and $ai=j$. Zero coefficients give $h=0$, covering split extensions; the proof made no smoothness or connectedness assumption.
